title: PostgreSQL DBA Part 22: Testing Backups with Restore Drills
description: Verify PostgreSQL backups with a real restore drill: pg_verifybackup, WAL chain checks, a drill cluster, pg_amcheck, pg_checksums and RTO.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery
PostgreSQL 18 docs: Write Ahead Log settings (recovery targets, archive_mode)

reviewNotes: Series part 22. Publish Part 21 first (Parts 18-21 are also not live yet; Part 21 is named without a link and is not in related). TEST ENVIRONMENT: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS. PostgreSQL 18 could NOT be installed: postgresql-18 18.7-1.pgdg24.04+5 from PGDG depends on liburing2 from the Ubuntu archive, which the sandbox network policy blocks (same as Parts 20-21). Every command ran on Ubuntu's PostgreSQL 16.15 (16.15-0ubuntu0.24.04.1), with the cluster created with --data-checksums to match the PostgreSQL 18 default, following the PostgreSQL 18.7 documentation (docs/18; note that postgresql.org/docs/current now shows version 19, so the sources point to /docs/18/). Paths in the article use 18 (16 replaced by 18); outputs that contain such paths are captioned expected output. I checked the PGDG 18 packages: pg_amcheck, pg_verifybackup, pg_checksums and pg_waldump are in /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin with no /usr/bin wrapper, and PGDG postgresql-common 297 does not override initdb options, so new 18 clusters get data checksums by default. All outputs are real from 16 (pg_verifybackup, pg_waldump gap error, recovery log, fingerprint diff, pg_amcheck with and without --install-missing, pg_checksums clean and with a deliberately damaged page in the drill copy, the pg_restore truncated-dump error, the drill script pass and the wrong-target FATAL). Possible differences on 18: the custom-format dump version, the exact wording of the checksum WARNING/ERROR (PostgreSQL 18 reworked read I/O), and file and block counts. NOT RUN: pgBackRest (the package needs libssh2 from the blocked Ubuntu archive), so the pgBackRest section has commands only, taken from the pgBackRest command reference, and no output; cron (not installed in the sandbox), the crontab lines were not run by cron but both scripts were run by hand with the same arguments; systemctl (no systemd), pg_ctlcluster was used, the article shows the equivalent systemctl commands. The script in Step 13 is the tested script with VER=16 changed to VER=18.

data.text: This is Part 22 of the PostgreSQL DBA series. In Part 21 we set up pgBackRest and ran our first restores with it. In this part you will learn how to verify a PostgreSQL backup properly: not only that the backup job said "completed", but that the backup restores, reaches the point in time you expect, and holds correct, uncorrupted data.

By the end you will be able to run a full restore drill on Ubuntu with PostgreSQL 18: check the backup files with pg_verifybackup, check the WAL chain with pg_waldump, restore into a throwaway cluster, compare the data with a saved reference, scan it for corruption with pg_amcheck and pg_checksums, measure how long it all took, and turn the whole drill into one script you can schedule every month.
What you will learn

items.content: The four levels of backup verification, and why a successful backup job proves very little on its own
How to check base backup files and the archived WAL chain without restoring anything
How to restore into a separate drill cluster and prove the data matches a saved reference
How to find corruption in a restored copy with pg_amcheck and pg_checksums
How to measure recovery time (RTO) and possible data loss (RPO), and automate the drill

data.text: Prerequisites

items.content: Parts 17 to 21 of this series: pg_dump and pg_restore, pg_basebackup, WAL archiving, point-in-time recovery and pgBackRest. This part reuses the same layout: base backups in /var/lib/postgresql/backups and archived WAL in /mnt/wal_archive.
One Ubuntu server (db1) with PostgreSQL 18 from the PGDG repository, cluster 18 main on port 5432, WAL archiving turned on as in Part 19.
Free disk space for one more full copy of the cluster, because the drill restores a complete copy on port 5433.
A user with sudo. Commands that touch PostgreSQL files run as the postgres operating system user.

data.text: How it works

A backup is a promise that you can get your data back. A restore drill is how you check the promise before you need it, the same way a fire drill checks that people can actually leave the building. The first real restore should never be the one you do during an outage.

Backups fail quietly. A WAL segment goes missing from the archive, a backup file is cut short when the disk fills, a disk flips a few bits, or a restore step only exists in the head of someone who has left the company. None of these shows up until you try to restore. So a DBA checks backups at four levels, from cheapest to most complete:

content: Did the backup and archiving finish without errors?
Are all backup files present and unchanged? Is the WAL chain complete?
Does the backup restore and replay WAL up to the target?
Is the restored data correct and free of corruption?

data.text: Only levels 3 and 4 really prove the backup. The PostgreSQL documentation says this directly about pg_verifybackup: even if you use it, you should still perform test restores and verify that the resulting databases work as expected and contain the correct data.

Two numbers come out of every drill. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long a restore takes, from the decision to restore until users can work again. RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you could lose, which for WAL archiving is roughly the age of the newest archived WAL segment. A drill measures your real RTO, and the archiver view shows your real RPO.

data.code:
db1 (10.0.0.11)

  cluster "18 main"  port 5432   production
        |  pg_basebackup              |  archive_command
        v                             v
  /var/lib/postgresql/backups/   /mnt/wal_archive/
        base_2026_11_20              000000010000000000000003 ...
        |                             |
        +--------- restore -----------+  restore_command
                       v
  cluster "18 drill" port 5433   throwaway copy: check, measure, drop
data.caption: The drill layout used in this part

data.title: Drill on a separate machine when you can
data.text: This part runs the drill on db1 to keep the lab small. A restore reads the whole backup and writes a full copy, which competes with production for disk and CPU. In production, run drills on a separate drill host that can read the backup storage. It also proves that you can restore when db1 is gone, which is the case backups exist for.
Prepare the lab
Step 1: Check archiving and data checksums

On db1, as postgres. A drill is only useful if the basics are on. Check that WAL archiving is working and that the cluster has data checksums. A data checksum is a small number stored in every 8 kB data page; PostgreSQL recalculates it when it reads the page, so a page changed by a faulty disk is detected instead of silently returning wrong data.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT name, setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name IN ('data_checksums','archive_mode','archive_command','archive_timeout') ORDER BY name;"
sudo -u postgres psql -x -c "SELECT archived_count, last_archived_wal, last_archived_time, failed_count, last_failed_wal FROM pg_stat_archiver;"

name       |                          setting
-----------------+------------------------------------------------------------
 archive_command | test ! -f /mnt/wal_archive/%f && cp %p /mnt/wal_archive/%f
 archive_mode    | on
 archive_timeout | 60
 data_checksums  | on
(4 rows)

-[ RECORD 1 ]------+-----------------------------
archived_count     | 1
last_archived_wal  | 000000010000000000000001
last_archived_time | 2026-11-20 12:48:22.18006+00
failed_count       | 0
last_failed_wal    |
data.caption: Output

data.text: data_checksums is read-only and shows whether the cluster was created with checksums. New in PostgreSQL 18: initdb enables data checksums by default, and Ubuntu's pg_createcluster uses that default, so a fresh 18 cluster shows on. Clusters created on PostgreSQL 17 or earlier without --data-checksums, and clusters upgraded from them, show off; pg_checksums --enable can turn checksums on later, but only while the server is stopped. failed_count must be 0 here. If it grows, fix archiving first (Part 19), because no drill can succeed with a broken archive.
Step 2: Create sample data
On db1, as postgres, in psql. We use a small shop database with two related tables and an index, so that the corruption checks later have tables and indexes to look at.

data.caption: Run in psql as postgres

data.text: Verify: SELECT count(*) FROM orders; in the shop database returns 50000.
Step 3: Take a base backup
On db1, as postgres. This is the same command as in Part 18. In real life you test the backups your scheduled job already made; we take one here so the lab is complete.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres mkdir -p /var/lib/postgresql/backups
sudo -u postgres pg_basebackup -D /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_2026_11_20 \
  --checkpoint=fast --label=base_2026_11_20 --progress

waiting for checkpoint
35483/35483 kB (100%), 0/1 tablespace
35483/35483 kB (100%), 1/1 tablespace
data.caption: Output

data.text: Verify: the backup_label file inside the backup shows the first WAL segment this backup needs. Write it down; you use it in Step 6.

data.code: sudo -u postgres head -2 /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_2026_11_20/backup_label

START WAL LOCATION: 0/3000028 (file 000000010000000000000003)
CHECKPOINT LOCATION: 0/3000060
data.caption: Output

data.text: Step 4: Save a reference fingerprint and a restore point

On db1, as postgres. To prove that restored data is correct, you need something to compare it with. A fingerprint is a short summary of table contents: the row count and an MD5 hash of all rows in key order. If even one value differs, the hash differs. Save the query in a file so you run exactly the same query on production and on the restored copy.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres mkdir -p /var/lib/postgresql/drill
sudo -u postgres tee /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql >/dev/null <<'EOF'
SELECT 'customers' AS table_name, count(*) AS row_count,
       md5(string_agg(c::text, ',' ORDER BY customer_id)) AS content_md5
  FROM customers AS c
UNION ALL
SELECT 'orders', count(*),
       md5(string_agg(o::text, ',' ORDER BY order_id))
  FROM orders AS o;
EOF

data.text: Now add some rows after the backup, so the drill must replay WAL to get them back. Then save the fingerprint and create a named restore point at the same moment. A restore point (Part 20) is a label in the WAL stream; recovery can stop exactly there, which makes the comparison exact.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop -c "INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, amount) SELECT 1 + g % 2000, 250.00 FROM generate_series(1, 5000) AS g;"
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql -o /var/lib/postgresql/drill/expected.txt
sudo -u postgres psql -Atc "SELECT pg_create_restore_point('drill_2026_11_20');"
sudo -u postgres cat /var/lib/postgresql/drill/expected.txt

data.text: 0/41BC420 is the WAL position of the restore point. Finally, keep working after the restore point and close the current WAL segment, so the archive holds everything:

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop -c "UPDATE orders SET amount = amount * 2 WHERE order_id <= 1000;"
sudo -u postgres psql -Atc "SELECT pg_switch_wal();"

data.title: Fingerprints on a busy server
data.text: Here nothing else writes to shop, so the fingerprint and the restore point describe the same data. On a busy production server rows can change between the two commands. There, fingerprint only data that no longer changes, for example orders WHERE created_at < current_date, and keep the query in the same file so both sides always run the same thing.
Check the backup files before restoring
Step 5: Verify the base backup with pg_verifybackup

On db1, as postgres. You met pg_verifybackup in Part 18. It reads the backup_manifest that the server wrote during the backup, checks that every file is present with the right size, recomputes each file's checksum, and parses the WAL the backup needs. It is in /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/, not in your PATH, so give the full path.

data.code: sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_verifybackup /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_2026_11_20; echo "exit=$?"

backup successfully verified
exit=0
data.caption: Output

data.text: Exit status 0 means no problems were found. Useful options from the reference page:

content: Print nothing when a backup is successfully verified (good for scripts)
Exit as soon as a problem is detected, instead of reporting all problems
Do not parse WAL. Needed for tar-format backups
Parse WAL from another directory, for example the WAL archive

data.text: The documentation is clear about the limits: pg_verifybackup finds missing files and changed contents, but it cannot run every check the server will run when it actually uses the backup. That is why the restore in Step 7 is still needed.
Step 6: Check that the archived WAL chain has no gaps

On db1, as postgres. A base backup alone only restores to the moment the backup ended. To reach any later point, recovery needs every WAL segment from the backup's start segment onwards, with no gap. pg_waldump (seen in Part 20) can read a range of segments from the archive; with --quiet it prints nothing unless it hits an error, such as a missing file.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres ls /mnt/wal_archive
sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_waldump --path=/mnt/wal_archive --quiet \
  000000010000000000000003 000000010000000000000004; echo "exit=$?"

content: Directory in which to find WAL segment files
Do not print any output, except for errors
The segment from backup_label (Step 3), where replay starts
The newest archived segment, shown as last_archived_wal in pg_stat_archiver

data.text: The file ending in .backup is the backup history file that PostgreSQL archives when a base backup finishes; it records the backup's start and stop WAL positions. For comparison, this is what a gap looks like. We copied segments 03 and 05 into a test directory but not 04:

data.code:
pg_waldump: error: could not find file "000000010000000000000004": No such file or directory
exit=1
data.caption: Output when a segment is missing

data.text: A gap means recovery can never get past that segment. Every point in time after it is lost until you take a new base backup.
Restore into a drill cluster
Step 7: Create an empty drill cluster and restore the backup

On db1, as a user with sudo. The procedure follows the recovery steps from Part 20 and the documentation: empty data directory, copy the base backup, remove old files from pg_wal, set restore_command and the target, create recovery.signal.

data.title: Check the path twice
data.text: The find ... -delete command permanently deletes everything in the directory you give it. Run it only on the new 18/drill directory, never on /var/lib/postgresql/18/main.

data.code:
date -u '+%F %T'
sudo pg_createcluster 18 drill --port 5433
sudo -u postgres find /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill -mindepth 1 -delete
sudo -u postgres cp -a /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_2026_11_20/. /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/
sudo -u postgres find /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/pg_wal -mindepth 1 -type f -delete
sudo -u postgres tee /etc/postgresql/18/drill/conf.d/drill.conf <<'EOF'
archive_mode = off
restore_command = 'cp /mnt/wal_archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_name = 'drill_2026_11_20'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'
EOF
sudo -u postgres touch /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/recovery.signal

data.caption: Output (first line: the drill start time, for the RTO)

content: The copy must never write its WAL into the production archive (/mnt/wal_archive). Can only be set at server start
How the drill fetches archived WAL segments; %f is the file name, %p the destination path
Stop at the restore point from Step 4. Recovery targets can only be set at server start
When the target is reached, finish recovery and accept connections. The default is pause

data.text: Verify: pg_lsclusters lists 18 drill 5433 down, and sudo -u postgres ls /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill shows backup_label, backup_manifest and recovery.signal.

data.title: Tablespaces
data.text: If the cluster uses tablespaces (Part 9), the backup's pg_tblspc folder holds symbolic links to other directories. Run ls -l /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/pg_tblspc before starting, and point every link at a separate copy. A link that points at production or at the backup itself lets the drill write there.
Step 8: Start the drill cluster and read the log
On db1, as a user with sudo.

data.code:
sudo systemctl start postgresql@18-drill
sudo tail -n 25 /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-drill.log

LOG:  database system was interrupted; last known up at 2026-11-20 12:48:36 UTC
cp: cannot stat '/mnt/wal_archive/00000002.history': No such file or directory
LOG:  starting point-in-time recovery to "drill_2026_11_20"
LOG:  starting backup recovery with redo LSN 0/3000028, checkpoint LSN 0/3000060, on timeline ID 1
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000003" from archive
LOG:  redo starts at 0/3000028
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000004" from archive
LOG:  completed backup recovery with redo LSN 0/3000028 and end LSN 0/3000100
LOG:  consistent recovery state reached at 0/3000100
LOG:  database system is ready to accept read-only connections
LOG:  recovery stopping at restore point "drill_2026_11_20", time 2026-11-20 12:48:41.785246+00
LOG:  redo done at 0/41BC3B8 system usage: CPU: user: 0.01 s, system: 0.00 s, elapsed: 0.06 s
LOG:  last completed transaction was at log time 2026-11-20 12:48:41.664731+00
LOG:  selected new timeline ID: 2
LOG:  archive recovery complete
LOG:  database system is ready to accept connections
data.caption: Output (tested on PostgreSQL 16; timestamps, process IDs, checkpoint and repeated history-file lines removed)

data.text: Read it from top to bottom: replay starts at the backup's start segment, the copy becomes consistent (the earliest moment it could be opened), recovery stops at the restore point, a new timeline 2 starts and the server accepts connections. The cp: cannot stat ... .history lines are normal: recovery asks the archive whether newer timelines exist, and none do.
Verify: the server must be out of recovery.

data.code: sudo -u postgres psql -p 5433 -Atc "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"
f
data.caption: Output

data.text: Note the time now. The difference from the start time in Step 7 is the restore part of your RTO. In this lab it was a few seconds; with hundreds of gigabytes it is mostly copy time plus WAL replay, and only a drill tells you the real number.
Prove the data is correct
Step 9: Compare the restored data with the reference
On db1, as postgres. Run the same fingerprint file on the drill cluster and compare it with the file saved in Step 4. diff prints nothing and returns 0 when the files are identical.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres psql -p 5433 -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql -o /var/lib/postgresql/drill/actual.txt
sudo -u postgres diff /var/lib/postgresql/drill/expected.txt /var/lib/postgresql/drill/actual.txt && echo "MATCH: restored data equals the reference"
MATCH: restored data equals the reference
data.caption: Output

data.text: For contrast, the same query on production now gives a different hash for orders, because of the UPDATE we ran after the restore point:

data.code: sudo -u postgres psql -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql

data.text: This proves two things at once: the restore brought back all 55,000 orders, and it stopped exactly at the restore point, not before or after.
Step 10: Scan the copy for corruption with pg_amcheck

On db1, as postgres. pg_amcheck runs the checks of the amcheck extension on every table and B-tree index: it reads table pages looking for damaged rows, and walks each index checking that it is internally consistent. Run it on the drill copy, not on production, so the extra reading costs production nothing.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_amcheck -p 5433 --all \
  --install-missing --heapallindexed --jobs=2; echo "exit=$?"
exit=0
data.caption: Output

content: Install any missing extensions required to check the databases (only amcheck); goes into pg_catalog by default
Also verify that every table row is present in each index. Takes several times longer
Use 2 connections to check objects in parallel

data.text: No output and exit status 0 means nothing was found. Two notes from the documentation: amcheck can only prove the presence of corruption, never its absence; and pg_amcheck checks tables, sequences, materialized views and B-tree indexes, silently skipping other index types. If you forget --install-missing, you get:

data.code:
pg_amcheck: warning: skipping database "postgres": amcheck is not installed
pg_amcheck: warning: skipping database "shop": amcheck is not installed
pg_amcheck: warning: skipping database "template1": amcheck is not installed
pg_amcheck: error: no relations to check
data.caption: Output without --install-missing

data.text: Step 11: Verify every data page checksum with pg_checksums

On db1, as a user with sudo. pg_checksums --check reads every data file and recomputes every page checksum. It is the most complete page-level check, but the documentation requires the server to be shut down cleanly first.

data.code:
sudo systemctl stop postgresql@18-drill
sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_checksums --check -D /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill; echo "exit=$?"

Checksum operation completed
Files scanned:   1255
Blocks scanned:  4406
Bad checksums:  0
Data checksum version: 1
exit=0
data.caption: Output

data.text: To see what a failure looks like, we overwrote 16 bytes in one page of the orders table file in the drill copy only and ran the checks again:

data.code:
pg_checksums: error: checksum verification failed in file "/var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/base/16384/16394", block 10: calculated checksum 47CF but block contains 4F21
Checksum operation completed
Files scanned:   1255
Blocks scanned:  4406
Bad checksums:  1
Data checksum version: 1
exit=1
data.caption: Output with one damaged page (expected output: tested on PostgreSQL 16, path shown for 18)

data.text: After starting the drill cluster, SELECT count(*) FROM orders; failed with the same problem, and pg_amcheck -p 5433 -d shop -t orders exited with status 2:

data.code:
WARNING:  page verification failed, calculated checksum 18383 but expected 20257
ERROR:  invalid page in block 10 of relation base/16384/16394
data.caption: Output (message wording can vary between versions)

data.text: If a drill finds this, do not delete the backup. Restore the previous backup to see whether the damage is older, run pg_amcheck on production at a quiet time, and check the disks. The checksum_failures column of pg_stat_database (Part 24) counts these errors per database, so monitor it on production too.
Step 12: Test a logical dump the same way

On db1, as postgres. pg_dump backups (Part 17) need their own drill. pg_restore --list only reads the table of contents at the start of the file, so it does not prove the file is complete. Restore it into a scratch database instead.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres pg_dump -Fc -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/backups/shop_2026_11_20.dump
sudo -u postgres createdb shop_drill
sudo -u postgres pg_restore -d shop_drill --exit-on-error /var/lib/postgresql/backups/shop_2026_11_20.dump; echo "exit=$?"
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql -o /tmp/prod.txt
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop_drill -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql -o /tmp/drill.txt
diff /tmp/prod.txt /tmp/drill.txt && echo "MATCH: dump restore equals production"

exit=0
MATCH: dump restore equals production
data.caption: Output

data.text: --exit-on-error makes pg_restore stop at the first SQL error; without it, errors are reported but the restore carries on, and you can miss them. We also cut a copy of the dump file in half to show why --list is not enough: pg_restore --list still returned 0, but the real restore failed:

data.code: pg_restore: error: could not read from input file: end of file
data.caption: Output when the dump file is truncated

data.text: Cleanup: sudo -u postgres dropdb shop_drill.
If you use pgBackRest

With pgBackRest from Part 21 the levels are the same, only the commands change. For level 2, the verify command checks that the backups and WAL archive in the repository are valid. By default it reports only errors; --verbose with --output=text also lists what was verified, and --set limits it to one backup set.

data.code: sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=app --output=text --verbose verify
data.caption: On db1, as postgres

data.text: For level 3, restore into the drill cluster's empty data directory with --type=immediate, which recovers only until the database becomes consistent, or with the default type, which replays to the end of the archive. Levels 3 and 4 then continue with Steps 8 to 11 exactly as above.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=app --pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/18/drill \
  --type=immediate --target-action=promote --archive-mode=off restore
data.caption: On db1, as postgres, after Step 7's pg_createcluster and find commands

data.text: Make the drill a routine
Step 13: Put the whole drill in one script

On db1, as a user with sudo. A drill that depends on someone remembering twelve steps will stop happening. The script below runs Step 5 and Steps 7 to 11 in order (add the Step 6 pg_waldump check with your own segment range if you like), stops at the first failure (set -euo pipefail), prints timings, and drops the drill cluster at the end. Save it as /usr/local/bin/restore-drill.sh and make it executable with sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/restore-drill.sh.

data.code:
#!/bin/bash
# restore-drill.sh: restore a base backup into a throwaway
# cluster "18 drill", verify it, report timings, then remove it.
# Run as root: sudo /usr/local/bin/restore-drill.sh <backup_dir> <restore_point>
set -euo pipefail
VER=18
BIN=/usr/lib/postgresql/$VER/bin
BACKUP=$1
TARGET=$2
DRILL=/var/lib/postgresql/$VER/drill
WORK=/var/lib/postgresql/drill
as_pg() { sudo -u postgres "$@"; }
log() { echo "$(date -u '+%F %T') $*"; }

log "drill start: backup=$BACKUP target=$TARGET"
T0=$(date +%s)

log "1/6 verify backup files"
as_pg $BIN/pg_verifybackup -q "$BACKUP"

log "2/6 create empty drill cluster on port 5433"
pg_dropcluster $VER drill --stop 2>/dev/null || true
pg_createcluster $VER drill --port 5433 >/dev/null
as_pg find "$DRILL" -mindepth 1 -delete

log "3/6 copy backup and configure recovery"
as_pg cp -a "$BACKUP/." "$DRILL/"
as_pg find "$DRILL/pg_wal" -mindepth 1 -type f -delete
as_pg tee /etc/postgresql/$VER/drill/conf.d/drill.conf >/dev/null <<CONF
archive_mode = off
restore_command = 'cp /mnt/wal_archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_name = '$TARGET'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'
CONF
as_pg touch "$DRILL/recovery.signal"

log "4/6 start and wait for recovery to finish"
pg_ctlcluster $VER drill start
for i in $(seq 1 600); do
  [ "$(as_pg psql -p 5433 -Atc 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()' 2>/dev/null)" = "f" ] && break
  pg_lsclusters -h $VER drill | grep -q online || break
  sleep 1
done
[ "$(as_pg psql -p 5433 -Atc 'SELECT pg_is_in_recovery()')" = "f" ]
T1=$(date +%s)
log "database open for writes after $((T1 - T0)) seconds"

log "5/6 compare data with the reference and run pg_amcheck"
as_pg psql -p 5433 -d shop -f $WORK/fingerprint.sql -o $WORK/actual.txt
as_pg diff $WORK/expected.txt $WORK/actual.txt
as_pg $BIN/pg_amcheck -p 5433 --all --install-missing --heapallindexed --jobs=2

log "6/6 stop and check data checksums"
pg_ctlcluster $VER drill stop
as_pg $BIN/pg_checksums --check -D "$DRILL" | grep 'Bad checksums'
pg_dropcluster $VER drill

log "DRILL PASSED in $(( $(date +%s) - T0 )) seconds"

data.text: The script uses pg_ctlcluster, which works the same as the systemctl commands in Steps 8 and 11. If the target is wrong or WAL is missing, the server stops during recovery, the wait loop sees the cluster go down, and the script exits with status 1 before printing PASSED. The cluster is left in place so you can read its log.
Step 14: Schedule it and keep a drill record
On db1, as a user with sudo. A monthly drill needs a fresh reference and restore point after the newest base backup. This small script saves both:

data.code:
#!/bin/bash
# drill-reference.sh: save the reference fingerprint and mark the
# matching point in the WAL stream for the next restore drill.
set -euo pipefail
sudo -u postgres psql -q -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql \
  -o /var/lib/postgresql/drill/expected.txt
sudo -u postgres psql -Atc "SELECT pg_create_restore_point('drill_monthly');"
data.caption: /usr/local/bin/drill-reference.sh

data.text: Then add two lines to root's crontab with sudo crontab -e: the reference at 02:00 and the drill at 03:00 on the first day of each month, after your nightly base backup has finished.

data.code:
#m h dom mon dow  command
0 2 1 * *  /usr/local/bin/drill-reference.sh
0 3 1 * *  /usr/local/bin/restore-drill.sh "$(ls -d /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_* | tail -1)" drill_monthly >> /var/log/restore-drill.log 2>&1
data.caption: root crontab

data.text: We ran the same pair by hand: drill-reference.sh printed the restore point position 0/80319D8, and the drill against drill_monthly ended with DRILL PASSED. Recovery stops at the first restore point with that name after the backup started, which is why the reference must run after the nightly backup. Verify: sudo crontab -l shows both lines, and on the second of the month tail /var/log/restore-drill.log ends with DRILL PASSED. Hook the log or the exit status into your alerting so a failure reaches a person.
For RPO, check the archiver on production. archive_age is roughly how much work you would lose if the server died now:

data.code: sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT last_archived_wal, last_archived_time, now() - last_archived_time AS archive_age, failed_count FROM pg_stat_archiver;"

data.text: With archive_timeout = 60 the age stays near or under a minute even when the server is quiet. Keep a short record of every drill: the date, the backup and target tested, the checks that passed, the measured RTO, and any problem found. Auditors ask for it, and the RTO trend tells you when backups are outgrowing your restore window.
Step 15: Clean up

On db1, as a user with sudo. The script already drops its cluster. If you followed Steps 7 to 11 by hand, remove the drill cluster; this deletes its data directory and its configuration in /etc/postgresql/18/drill.

data.code:
sudo pg_dropcluster 18 drill --stop
pg_lsclusters

Ver Cluster Port Status Owner    Data directory              Log file
18  main    5432 online postgres /var/lib/postgresql/18/main /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-18-main.log

data.text: Common mistakes and how to fix them
FATAL: recovery ended before configured recovery target was reached
Recovery replayed all the WAL it could find but never met the target. We got this by giving the drill a restore point name that does not exist:

data.code:
LOG:  restored log file "000000010000000000000006" from archive
cp: cannot stat '/mnt/wal_archive/000000010000000000000007': No such file or directory
LOG:  redo done at 0/62F4628 system usage: CPU: user: 0.01 s, system: 0.01 s, elapsed: 0.13 s
LOG:  last completed transaction was at log time 2026-11-20 12:49:37.287163+00
FATAL:  recovery ended before configured recovery target was reached
data.caption: Output

data.text: Fix: check the spelling of the restore point, that the target time is after the backup ended, and that the archive holds WAL up to the target (Step 6). If a segment is genuinely missing, the target cannot be reached from this backup; take a new base backup today.
pg_checksums: error: cluster must be shut down
You ran pg_checksums --check while the drill cluster was running. Fix: sudo systemctl stop postgresql@18-drill first. Never run it against a running production data directory.
The drill wrote WAL into the production archive

You left archive_mode on in the drill cluster, so after promotion it archived its own timeline 2 files into /mnt/wal_archive. Fix: always set archive_mode = off in the drill configuration (Step 7, or --archive-mode=off with pgBackRest), and if it already happened, remove only the files the drill created, such as 00000002.history and segments starting with 00000002.
Trusting the backup job's exit code alone

A job can finish with status 0 while archiving has been failing for days, or while a dump was written to a disk that later filled. Fix: alert on pg_stat_archiver.failed_count and archive_age, run pg_verifybackup after every backup, and run the full drill at least monthly and after every change to backup tooling, storage or PostgreSQL version.
Practice exercise

items.content: Copy your WAL archive into a test directory, delete one segment from the middle of the copy, and run the Step 6 pg_waldump command against the copy. Which message do you get, and what is the newest point you could still recover to?
Change the drill to use recovery_target = 'immediate' instead of the restore point. Does the fingerprint still match the one from Step 4? Why or why not?

data.title: Answers
data.text: 1. pg_waldump prints could not find file followed by the missing segment name and exits with 1. You can recover only up to the end of the last segment before the gap. 2. It does not match: 'immediate' stops as soon as the copy is consistent, which is the end of the base backup, so the 5,000 orders inserted after the backup are missing (row_count 50000 instead of 55000). Use immediate to test the backup alone, and a restore point or time to test the backup plus WAL.
Quick reference

data.code:
# Level 1: archiving healthy, checksums on (production)
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SHOW data_checksums;"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "SELECT last_archived_wal, now() - last_archived_time AS archive_age, failed_count FROM pg_stat_archiver;"

# Reference fingerprint and restore point (production)
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql -o /var/lib/postgresql/drill/expected.txt
sudo -u postgres psql -Atc "SELECT pg_create_restore_point('drill_2026_11_20');"

# Level 2: backup files and WAL chain
sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_verifybackup /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_2026_11_20
sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_waldump --path=/mnt/wal_archive --quiet <first_segment> <last_segment>

# Level 3: restore into the drill cluster
sudo pg_createcluster 18 drill --port 5433
sudo -u postgres find /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill -mindepth 1 -delete
sudo -u postgres cp -a /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_2026_11_20/. /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/
sudo -u postgres find /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/pg_wal -mindepth 1 -type f -delete
# write /etc/postgresql/18/drill/conf.d/drill.conf (archive_mode, restore_command, target, action)
sudo -u postgres touch /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill/recovery.signal
sudo systemctl start postgresql@18-drill
sudo -u postgres psql -p 5433 -Atc "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();"

# Level 4: data correct and uncorrupted
sudo -u postgres psql -p 5433 -d shop -f /var/lib/postgresql/drill/fingerprint.sql -o /var/lib/postgresql/drill/actual.txt
sudo -u postgres diff /var/lib/postgresql/drill/expected.txt /var/lib/postgresql/drill/actual.txt
sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_amcheck -p 5433 --all --install-missing --heapallindexed --jobs=2
sudo systemctl stop postgresql@18-drill
sudo -u postgres /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_checksums --check -D /var/lib/postgresql/18/drill

# Logical dump drill
sudo -u postgres createdb shop_drill
sudo -u postgres pg_restore -d shop_drill --exit-on-error /var/lib/postgresql/backups/shop_2026_11_20.dump

# pgBackRest repository check
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=app --output=text --verbose verify

# Whole drill in one go, and cleanup
sudo /usr/local/bin/restore-drill.sh /var/lib/postgresql/backups/base_2026_11_20 drill_2026_11_20
sudo pg_dropcluster 18 drill --stop

data.text: Summary and what's next

items.content: A backup is only proven when it has been restored and its data checked
Level 2: pg_verifybackup for base backups, pg_waldump --quiet for the WAL chain, pgbackrest verify for a pgBackRest repository
Level 3: restore into a separate drill cluster with archive_mode = off and a precise recovery target
Level 4: compare a saved fingerprint, then run pg_amcheck and pg_checksums on the copy, never load production with them
Restore pg_dump files into a scratch database with --exit-on-error; pg_restore --list is not a test
Script the drill, schedule it monthly, alert on failure, and record the measured RTO every time

data.text: In Part 23 we move from backups to monitoring and set up logging that helps: log_min_duration_statement, log_line_prefix and auto_explain.

linkedin.post:
Your backup job says "completed". That proves less than you think.

A backup is only proven when you have restored it and checked the data inside. In Part 22 of my PostgreSQL DBA series I built a restore drill you can run every month:

1. pg_verifybackup checks every file in a base backup against its manifest and checksums.
2. pg_waldump --quiet over the archive finds a missing WAL segment before a real recovery does.
3. Restore into a throwaway cluster on another port, with archive_mode = off and a named restore point as the target.
4. Compare a saved fingerprint (row count plus md5 of all rows) with the restored copy, then run pg_amcheck and pg_checksums on the copy, not on production.
5. Script it, schedule it, and record how long the restore took. That number is your real RTO.

One surprise from testing: pg_restore --list happily read a dump file cut in half. Only a real restore failed with "end of file".

When did you last restore one of your production backups, and how long did it take?

Full tutorial with examples: link in the first comment.

2. Files: backup and WAL chain complete
3. Restore: the backup replays to the target
4. Data: correct and free of corruption

points: pg_verifybackup checks files against the manifest
pg_waldump --quiet over the archive finds WAL gaps
slides.code:
SELECT last_archived_wal,
  now() - last_archived_time
    AS archive_age,
  failed_count
FROM pg_stat_archiver;

slides.title: Level 3: restore into a drill
points: New cluster on port 5433, copy the base backup
archive_mode = off so it never touches the archive
Stop at a named restore point, then promote

slides.title: Level 4: prove the data
slides.body: Save a fingerprint before the restore point, run the same query on the copy and diff the two files. Then run pg_amcheck and pg_checksums on the copy.
slides.code:
SELECT count(*) AS row_count,
  md5(string_agg(o::text, ','
      ORDER BY order_id))
FROM orders AS o;

slides.title: Make it routine
points: Script every step and stop at the first failure
Schedule it monthly and alert when it fails
Record the restore time: that is your real RTO
pg_restore --list is not a test of a dump file
